title: How does consulting recruiting work, from application to offer?
description: The typical stages of consulting recruiting for students and experienced hires: applications, tests, interview rounds, timing and what each stage screens for.
hook: Consulting recruiting follows the same basic funnel at almost every firm: research and networking, an application, an online assessment, a first round of interviews, a final round, then an offer. Each stage screens for something different, so you prepare for each in a different way. Once you see the shape and track your own progress through it, the process becomes far less daunting.
body:
In this guide

  • The usual stages
  • What each stage screens for
  • Timing for students and experienced hires
  • A worked example: reading your own funnel
  • Two workstreams: getting selected and performing
  • Common mistakes
  • Practise now
  • Where to go next

The usual stages

  1. Research and networking. Learning what each firm does and talking to people who work there. How to network without feeling awkward.
  2. Application. A CV, often a cover letter, sometimes transcripts. How to write a consulting CV.
  3. Online assessment. Depending on the firm: a game-based problem-solving test, an online case, numerical and logical reasoning tests, a situational judgement test or recorded video answers. How to prepare for online tests.
  4. First round. Usually two interviews, each combining a case with fit or experience questions.
  5. Final round. Two or three interviews with more senior people. Some firms or offices add a written case, a group exercise or a presentation.
  6. Offer. Often within days of the final round.

The details vary, and the firms' own pages show how. McKinsey describes a gamified assessment, Solve, used for most consulting roles, followed by problem-solving (case) interviews and Personal Experience Interviews. Bain says consulting applicants typically take a digital assessment and then case interviews. KPMG UK's graduate route runs online tests, then a recorded video interview, then a half-day assessment event, with offers within two working days. Deloitte Australia's student process ends in an assessment day that can include a group case study and a one-to-one interview. Our firm-by-firm guides cover each process in detail.

What each stage screens for

StageWhat it screens forHow to prepare
CV and cover letterAcademic strength, achievement, leadershipResults-led bullets; a specific reason for each firm
Online assessmentProblem solving and numeracy under time pressureTimed practice of the exact format
Case interviewsStructure, maths, judgement, communicationLive cases with a partner, plus drills
Fit interviewsMotivation, impact, leadership, how you work with peopleA bank of six to eight detailed stories
Final roundAll of the above, plus whether seniors want you on their teamConsistency under fatigue; a clear "why us"

Notice that the early stages are about getting selected and the later ones about performing. That split matters for how you spend your time.

Timing for students and experienced hires

Students

Many firms recruit students on an annual cycle, with deadlines for internships and graduate roles months before the start date. Internships are a common route to full-time offers. Some firms recruit on a rolling basis, so places can fill before the official deadline; KPMG UK, for example, says so explicitly. Dates differ by country, office and programme, so build your own calendar from each firm's careers page.

An illustrative timeline for one cycle:

  • Months 1 to 2: research firms, attend events, talk to people, polish your CV, start case practice.
  • Month 3: applications and online tests.
  • Months 3 to 4: first rounds, then final rounds, often a week or two apart.
  • Month 4: offers.

Experienced hires

Recruiting is usually rolling rather than seasonal. It often starts with a recruiter conversation and may include interviews about your industry expertise as well as cases. Some firms ask you to choose one office; L.E.K., for instance, lets you apply to only one of its offices a year. Roland Berger suggests applying three to four months before your ideal start date.

A worked example: reading your own funnel

Treat your applications as a funnel, not a verdict on your worth. Track each firm and team, your contact there, application date, test result, interview stage and next action. Then look at the conversion between stages. Here is an illustrative season:

StageNumberConversion from previous stage
Applications30n/a
Invited to online test1240%
First-round interviews650%
Final rounds233%
Offers150%

One offer from 30 applications is about 3%. The overall rate matters less than where you drop out. Here the weakest step is first round to final round: two of six. That points to case or fit performance, not the CV. The fix is more live cases with feedback and sharper stories, not another 20 applications.

Compare a different pattern: 30 applications and only two invitations to anything. The problem is now positioning: the CV, the roles you are targeting or the lack of a contact at the firm. Doing more mock cases will not help an application that never reaches an interviewer.

Two workstreams: getting selected and performing

Run two workstreams in parallel from the start.

  • Getting selected: a results-focused CV, well-chosen roles, outreach to people at each firm and a specific motivation for each one.
  • Performing once selected: numerical fluency, leading a case, communicating clearly and telling detailed fit stories.

Most people need several weeks of steady case practice. The three-week plan is a good starting point once you have interviews booked, with a six-week version if you are starting early. Keep a bank of application stories, but edit the proof points and the motivation for each firm and team.

Weak "why us": "You are one of the most prestigious firms and the exit opportunities are excellent."
Strong "why us": "I want to work on healthcare operations. Your team's hospital work came up in both conversations I had with people in the London office, and it builds directly on my placement analysing clinic waiting times."

Common mistakes

  • Starting case practice after the invitation arrives. The gap between invitation and interview can be a week or two. Start early.
  • Missing rolling deadlines. Apply as soon as you are ready, not on the closing date.
  • Preparing only cases. Fit questions and online tests knock out many strong case solvers.
  • Copy-paste motivation. Interviewers notice when your "why us" could fit any firm.
  • Not asking for feedback. After a rejection, ask politely. What to do after a rejection.

Practise now

1. You sent 40 applications, 30 invited you to online tests, but only 3 invited you to first rounds. Where is the problem?

Show the answer

Application to test is 75%, which is healthy, so the CV is working. Test to first round is 3 ÷ 30 = 10%, so the online assessment is the bottleneck. Practise the exact test formats under time pressure before applying to more firms.

2. You reached four final rounds and received no offers. What should you do next?

Show the answer

You are clearly good enough to get to the end, so look for a repeated weakness late in the process. Ask each firm for feedback, write a debrief of every final round, and look for patterns: running out of energy in the third interview, a thin "why us", or weaker recommendations. Then practise exactly that, ideally with someone senior.

3. It is September and the internship deadlines you care about close in eight weeks. How do you split your time?

Show the answer

Weeks 1 to 3: CV, research and two or three conversations per firm, with light case practice. Weeks 4 to 6: applications as soon as each is ready, plus timed online test practice. Weeks 7 to 8: daily cases and fit stories, so you are ready when invitations arrive. Both workstreams run throughout; only the balance shifts.

Where to go next

If you are new to cases, start with how to prepare for case interviews from scratch, then practise with real cases from the PrepForCase casebook. Details on firm processes were checked in November 2026; always confirm with each firm.
